deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It is a heavily corrected draft of the opening of Riemann's epistemological fragment 'Versuch einer Lehre von den Grundbegriffen der Mathematik und Physik als Grundlage für die Naturerklärung'. A version of it was published posthumously by Dedekind and Weber in the Gesammelte Werke, under the philosophical fragments ('Erkenntnisstheoretisches').

The argument runs as follows.
(a) Natural science is defined as the attempt to grasp nature through exact concepts (Begriffe).
(b) Through such a concept system, current perceptions are completed. Future perceptions are determined in advance as necessary or, where the system is incomplete, as probable. The system also fixes what is really possible, necessary or impossible. If the concepts are exact enough, the degree of possibility (probability) of each event can be determined mathematically.
(c) When what is predicted occurs, the system is confirmed. Our trust in it rests on this confirmation by experience.
(d) When something occurs that the system calls impossible or improbable, the task arises to complete or rework it, so that the perceived event ceases to be impossible or improbable. Through this process our grasp of nature becomes ever more complete and correct. At the same time it reaches ever further behind the surface of appearances. This completion or correction constitutes the 'explanation' of the unexpected perception.
(e) Hence there are two sources of concepts:
  1. formation of concepts from perceptions by abstraction;
  2. transformation or completion of existing concepts to remove contradictions or improbabilities.
(f) The history of the explanatory sciences shows that present concept systems arose from gradual transformation of older ones. The motives for new explanations always trace back to contradictions or improbabilities in the older ones.
(g) Herbart is credited with having shown the same for concepts whose origin we cannot trace historically or in our own development, because they are passed on unnoticed with language. As far as they are more than mere forms of connecting simple sensory representations, they derive from these sources. They need no a priori constitution of the soul, 'such as Kant's categories'.
(h) This proof of their origin matters for natural science, because only so can their meaning be fixed adequately through sense perception. The psychological process of concept formation is not laid out here.
(i) The two sources are restated at the foot of the page.

Read in modern terms, this is a fallibilist, quasi-Bayesian picture: theories assign probabilities to events and are revised when improbable events are observed. The next page continues with the concept of independently existing things. It derives continuous change and causality from the demand to keep that concept as far as possible.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since the page has no computations.
The probabilistic claim (degrees of possibility are mathematically determinable if the concepts are exact enough) is asserted programmatically, not argued.
The empirical claim that the reasons for new explanations can 'always' be traced to contradictions or improbabilities is a sweeping historical generalisation without support on the page.

results.what: Science as a system of exact concepts that predicts perceptions as necessary or probable, is confirmed by experience, and is revised when improbable or impossible observations occur.
results.modern_name: Hypothetico-deductive / fallibilist philosophy of science, with a probabilistic (proto-Bayesian) confirmation idea
results.usually_credited_to: Various: Herschel, Whewell (1840), later Peirce, Popper, Bayesian confirmation theory

results.what: Two sources of concepts: abstraction from perception, and transformation of concepts to remove contradictions or improbabilities; Herbartian rejection of Kant's a priori categories.
results.modern_name: Herbartian empiricist theory of concept formation (Bearbeitung der Begriffe)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart; Riemann's version is known from the Werke (Dedekind/Weber 1876)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known opening of Riemann's published epistemological fragment, printed in the Gesammelte Werke. Its Herbartian character and the explicit anti-Kantian remark are thoroughly discussed in the literature (e.g. E. Scholz, J. Ferreirós). It contains no mathematics; only draft variants and deletions are new relative to the printed text.
transcription_corrections: Line on gradual improvement: the surviving (uncrossed) sense matches the published text: 'Durch diesen Process wird unsere Auffassung der Natur allmählich immer vollständiger und richtiger, geht aber zugleich immer mehr hinter die Oberfläche der Erscheinungen zurück.' The machine transcription garbles this into two incomplete sentences.
'weil sie mit unvermerkt mit der Sprache überliefert werden' should read 'weil sie unvermerkt mit der Sprache überliefert werden' (duplicated 'mit').
'Nun werden wir nachzuweisen [?] versuchen' should probably read 'Wir werden nun nachzuweisen versuchen' or similar; this line is heavily reworked.
The final 'Erklärung' sentence: 'unerwarteten Wahrnehmung', with 'Erfahrung' as an interlinear alternative placed above; the reading order in the transcription is inverted.
The '(88)' is the archival folio stamp, not part of Riemann's text.
